symptom: A workflow user task whose task page takes the context entity instead of System.WorkflowUserTask (CE7412), takes no parameters (CE7410), or whose targeting microflow does not take exactly System.Workflow plus the context entity (CE6677) passed `mxcli check` AND `check --references`, was written by exec, and failed only under the native mx check. Reported in a team briefing on building workflows from MDL as two of the reasons 'a green CLI check is not evidence for workflows'.
cause: validateWorkflowReferences resolved the user task's page and targeting microflow by NAME only — it reported a document that does not exist, never one that exists with the wrong signature. Neither signature was in `mxcli syntax workflow` either, so authors had nothing to copy.
fix: validate_workflow_task_signature.go checks both signatures from the script's own definitions first (scriptContext now records page parameter entities and entity generalizations, beside flowParams) and then the project, for CREATE WORKFLOW (incl. nested and multi-user tasks) and ALTER WORKFLOW (inserted tasks, SET ACTIVITY PAGE / TARGETING MICROFLOW, context entity read off the stored workflow). Wired into validateWorkflowStatementRefs / validateAlterWorkflowRefs. check --references reports before anything is written; exec calls the same function at the workflow statement, so the workflow is never written but earlier statements in the script already are. Gated on Mendix 11, where it is measured.
insight: Measure the CLEAN edges before writing a refusal — three of the nine rows would have been false refusals from a plausible reading of the error text: a task page MAY take extra parameters besides WorkflowUserTask, a targeting microflow MAY take its two parameters in either order, and its context parameter MAY be a generalization of the context entity (but not a specialization). Since exec refuses on a check error, a false refusal is a blocker. Where the inheritance chain leaves what can be resolved (a script entity extending something unknown), return 'not proven' rather than a mismatch. Also a harness caveat worth keeping: the control run that stubbed the version gate first reported 0 failures because the harness only counted `--- FAIL` lines containing '/', i.e. subtests; the gate test is top-level. A silent control is a claim about the harness before it is a claim about the test. And run `make test-integration` before pushing a reference-path rule: the unit suite gates the rule on a mock project with no version, so it never fired there, while the integration round-trip tests exec against a real 11.x project — and their shared helper created task pages with no parameters and targeting microflows with none, which CI refused. Those fixtures had never been built; the rule was right, they were repaired.
